tagline: Rolling ridge tops connect working farms with Danish and German Iowa
intro: Western Skies follows rolling hills and ridge tops through western Iowa, linking working farmsteads and rural towns. The paved, 142-mile byway parallels Interstate 80 and connects with Interstate 29. Golden Hills RC&D, its coordinating organization, presents the drive as a journey through Iowa’s agricultural past and cultural heritage. Its suggested itineraries span one or two days. Travel Iowa points to German churches in Westphalia and Panama and the Danish villages of Elk Horn and Kimballton as expressions of that heritage along the route.

Dedicated in 1998, Western Skies was among Iowa’s first state-designated scenic byways. The designation gathered 14 rural towns across Harrison, Shelby, Audubon and Guthrie counties into one corridor. Those towns include Westphalia, founded in 1872 by German Catholic farmers and small merchants, and Elk Horn, where a Danish folk school drew immigrants beginning in 1878.

Start near Missouri Valley on Highway 30, then choose Highway 44 or the northern loop through Woodbine and County Road F32; both reach Harlan. Continue east to Kimballton, with Elk Horn on a southbound Highway 173 spur. Back on Highway 44, the rolling ridge top leads through Hamlin and Guthrie Center to Panora, where P28 turns south to Stuart. The western loop and Elk Horn spur offer different branches of the drive before the route’s eastern finish at Interstate 80.

moments.title: Westphalia
moments.text: Westphalia began in 1872 as a colony of German Catholic farmers and small merchants. They named it for Germany’s Province of Westphalia. The town’s German heritage is visible in a church built by its founders, one of the architectural features Travel Iowa highlights along this route.

moments.title: Elk Horn
moments.text: Elk Horn’s Danish connections run through education as well as its working windmill. In 1878, Danish immigrant Kristian Ostergaard founded the Elk Horn Højskole, America’s first Danish folk school. The school attracted Danish immigrants, and in 1894 its owner, Pastor Kristian Anker, sold it to the Danish Lutheran Church in North America for a seminary and college. The seminary moved to Nebraska in 1896. Elk Horn now houses the Museum of Danish America and a working Danish windmill. Danish cooking remains part of the town’s life, with businesses making and selling Danish bakery goods.

moments.title: Stuart
moments.text: Stuart grew with the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad in the late 1860s. Captain Charles Stuart helped bring the railroad here and founded the city that carries his name. The settlement was platted in 1870 and incorporated in 1887. Its railroad connection is represented on the National Register of Historic Places by the Stuart Passenger Station, dated 1869. The byway ends here, at the town where Bonnie and Clyde staged their last bank robbery. The town’s former All Saints Catholic Church and Masonic Temple Building are also listed on the National Register.
